text: If the patient reports any swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, always ask about breathing difficulty next, since this combination is a hallmark of a severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) requiring emergency attention.

Ask specifically about anything new in the last 24 hours — a new medication, a new food, or an insect sting — since identifying the likely trigger is one of the most clinically useful pieces of information for an allergic reaction visit.
If the patient has had a similar reaction before, ask whether an epinephrine auto-injector (EpiPen) was used or prescribed at that time, since this indicates how severe past reactions have been.
Ask whether the rash or reaction is spreading or getting worse, since a rapidly spreading reaction is more urgent than one that is stable or improving.
